options: Add more adjectives to the subject description
Add the exclusion block: morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker
Switch to a higher resolution
Generate three variations and pick the best
questions.q: Your first generation comes back with a morphing face and melting hands. Which prompt layer was missing?
questions.why: The exclusion block names what breaks cinematic output, morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker. The chapter says to put it in every prompt, not just the risky ones.

options: Re-describe the face in even more detail for safety
Drop the Soul ID and use a text description instead
Describe only what changes: wardrobe, setting, action, expression, camera, light, style
Generate the face separately and composite it in post
questions.q: You're directing a Soul ID character and re-describing her face in detail in every shot's prompt. What's wrong?
questions.why: The Soul ID prompting rule: when a Soul ID character is active, do not re-describe the face or core features, the Soul ID handles that. Describe only what changes.

options: Split it: one believable action per clip
Add the exclusion block and try again
Use a longer duration so all four actions fit
Describe the actions faster with shorter sentences
questions.q: One 5-second clip asks the character to enter the room, sit down, pick up the phone, and answer it. What breaks, and what's the fix?
questions.why: Per-shot discipline: one shot = one fully self-contained prompt, one action per clip. Four actions in five seconds guarantees none of them land.

options: Text-to-video, because it gives the model more creative freedom
Text-to-video, because start frames slow you down
Either, the chapter says they're equivalent for control
Image-to-video: generate the still, approve it, then animate
questions.q: You need precise control over a product shot. Which does the chapter recommend?
questions.why: Image-to-video (start frame first) beats text-to-video for control. Generate the still, approve it, then animate.

options: "Zoom in" is fine, the models understand it
Use motivated, physical phrasing: "the camera slowly dollies toward the subject with smooth stabilized movement", every move needs a purpose
Stack three camera moves so one of them lands
Avoid camera language entirely and let the model decide
questions.q: Your camera direction just says "zoom in." What does the chapter recommend instead?
questions.why: "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in." Rule: every movement needs a purpose, ask what the move reveals or withholds.

options: Increase the lighting contrast on the face
Add "cinematic, emotional" to the style layer
Give the eyes a job: name an eyeline target per beat, eyes move between targets, never stare into the middle distance
Use a tighter close-up so the eyes are bigger in frame
questions.q: Your AI actor's performance feels dead, glassy, unfocused eyes. What's the first fix?
questions.why: The chapter's highest-leverage note: dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting, they're fixed by giving the eyes a job. Name the eyeline target per beat; if a performance feels dead, check the eyes first.

options: Break the turn into separate shots, the turn happens in the cut; one feeling per shot
Write a longer, more emotional prompt so the arc fits in the clip
Use the exclusion block to remove the flat expression
Generate at higher resolution for more facial detail
questions.q: A single 6-second clip needs the character to go from hopeful to devastated. How do you direct it?
questions.why: One feeling per shot: AI can't play an arc inside a single clip. It can hold one tactic for 4 to 8 seconds. Break emotional turns into separate shots.

options: Make the speaker's prompt longer and more detailed
Add dialogue audio in the same generation
Switch to a more expensive model tier
Cut to the listener: the listener's eyes do half the acting, AI renders listening better than complex feeling
questions.q: A dialogue scene feels flat even though the speaker's lines are well prompted. What's the chapter's fix?
questions.why: In dialogue coverage, the listener's eyes do half the acting. The reaction shot is your best friend: AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling.

options: Use them for every emotional beat, faces are the model's strength
Ration them: close-ups magnify every flaw, so spend them where they count
Avoid them entirely; only use wide shots
Use them only for dialogue, never for silent moments
questions.q: How should you deploy close-ups in an AI-directed scene?
questions.why: Micro-acting is the weakest link in every current model. Spend close-ups at emotional peaks, that's where the audience looks hardest and where the model fails most visibly. Wides and mediums carry the rest.

options: Generate the whole scene in one long take
Describe the full emotional arc in a single prompt and let the model pace it
Direct in passes: rehearsal is drafts, generate, judge, adjust the tactic, re-shoot the beat
Lock the first acceptable take and never iterate
questions.q: Your dialogue scene isn't landing after the first generation. What's the directing discipline?
questions.why: Rehearsal is drafts. AI directing is iterative: generate the beat, read it like a director, adjust one thing (the tactic, the eyeline, the framing), and re-shoot.

options: Trained identity (Soul ID) > character-sheet reference > per-generation reference > text description alone
Text description alone > per-generation reference > character sheet > trained identity
Per-generation reference > trained identity > text description > character sheet
They're all equally reliable if the prompt is detailed
questions.q: Rank the identity stack from most to least reliable for holding a face across 50 shots.
questions.why: The ranked identity stack: trained identity (Soul ID) is the gold standard; then character sheet as reference; then per-generation reference upload; text description alone is weakest, never rely on prose to hold a face across 50 shots.

options: Describe the jacket slightly differently each time for variety
Let the model improvise wardrobe from the character's personality
Write the wardrobe once in exact language and paste it verbatim into every prompt
Fix wardrobe drift in the grade
questions.q: Your character's jacket changes shade between shots. What's the fix?
questions.why: Wardrobe lock: write the wardrobe once, in exact language, and paste it verbatim into every prompt. Props get the same treatment.

options: Generate a fresh start frame for visual variety
Start from the last frame of the previous approved clip, never fabricate a start frame
Start from the first frame of the scene for consistency
Use text-to-video so the model invents the transition
questions.q: Shot 12 must continue shot 11's action seamlessly. What starts the generation?
questions.why: Last-frame chaining: every clip starts from the last frame of the previous approved clip. Never fabricate a start frame.

options: Chain it anyway, minor drift is invisible in motion
Fix it in the edit with a quick cutaway
Keep it for B-roll
Reject it: failed clips don't chain, they get re-prompted
questions.q: A clip comes back with the face drifting and the light flipped from the scene's lock. What do you do with it?
questions.why: Rejection rules: a clip fails if the face drifts, wardrobe changes, the light flips, or the camera moves without motivation. Failed clips don't chain, they get re-prompted.

options: Generate and approve a master still of each location first; every shot starts from it or references it
Describe the location fresh in each prompt for richness
Rely on the model's memory of earlier clips
Shoot all location shots in one batch and hope
questions.q: The location looks different in every shot of your film. What's the chapter's system?
questions.why: World consistency: generate and approve a master still of each location first. Every shot in that location starts from it or references it. Same for lighting continuity, lock time of day and light direction per scene.

options: It's realistic, the models are that reliable now
Double it to be safe
It's a fiction: the documented regime is 5 to 20x regeneration overhead, tens of thousands of assets per finished minute
It only applies to dialogue-heavy films
questions.q: Your budget spreadsheet for a 20-minute short assumes every second generated exactly once (the "clean pass"). What's wrong?
questions.why: The clean pass is a fiction in practice. The documented regime is 5 to 20x regeneration overhead, the chapter cites 41,118 assets for 20 finished minutes.

options: Sequence assembly, parallel teams are always better
Scene-by-scene, one director, chained folders, tight control (the ONEIRIC pattern)
Generate the whole film as one prompt
Whichever is cheaper per credit
questions.q: You're a solo creator making a 20-minute short with a single strong vision. Which build architecture fits?
questions.why: Two documented architectures: scene-by-scene (ONEIRIC's video-chained per-scene folders, tight directorial control, fits solo/small teams) vs. sequence assembly (parallel teams with version logs, throughput at scale, fits crews).

options: Native audio only, it's the simplest
Human-recorded dialogue, then AI-converted (the Koosha 75-minute-feature pattern) or decoupled TTS, dialogue at scale needs a controllable pipeline
Generate dialogue natively and accept whatever comes out
Skip dialogue entirely; use title cards
questions.q: You're planning a 75-minute feature with heavy dialogue. Which dialogue architecture does the chapter document for this scale?
questions.why: Three architectures: native audio (Seedance), human-recorded then AI-converted (Koosha's 75-min feature), decoupled TTS. At feature scale with heavy dialogue, you need a controllable pipeline, native generation doesn't survive 75 minutes of lip-sync.

options: ~$38, one clean pass at $1.90/min
It can't be estimated
~$1,900 flat regardless of overhead
~$190 to $750 at 5 to 20x overhead (clean pass ~$1.90/min is the fiction), and verify live, rates move monthly
questions.q: What's the chapter's documented cost envelope for a 20-minute film on Kling 2.5 Turbo?
questions.why: Clean $1.90/finished minute is the fiction; the real envelope is ~$190 to $750 at 5 to 20x overhead. And rates move monthly, verify live before budgeting.

options: Nothing, long-form is a solved problem now
Only the cost
The subtle-acting ceiling, cumulative drift across scenes, and asset counts that break undisciplined pipelines
Only render times
questions.q: What does the chapter list as the honest limits, what still breaks at 20+ minutes?
questions.why: Honest limits: the subtle-acting ceiling (AI still can't do restrained interior performance), cumulative drift over long runtimes, and the asset-count reality that breaks undisciplined pipelines.

options: Keep it, native audio is the final mix
Strip the dialogue and build it deliberately on its own track; keep native audio only as ambient texture
Delete all native audio on principle
Use it only if the lip-sync is perfect
questions.q: Your video model generated a clip with native audio including dialogue. What do you do with the dialogue?
questions.why: Treat native audio as raw material, never as the mix: keep it for ambient texture (room tone, wind, footsteps); strip dialogue, music, anything prominent, those get built deliberately on their own tracks.

questions.q: You're casting a synthetic voice for a character across 40 shots. What's the chapter's discipline?
options: Use a different voice per scene for variety
Write a Voice Bible for the character and choose the dialogue route per scene, native or decoupled, never mixed mid-scene
Generate the voice fresh each shot; the model remembers the character
Use whatever default voice the TTS platform suggests
questions.why: The audio checklist: a Voice Bible written and referenced for every speaking character, and the dialogue route chosen per scene, native or decoupled, never mixed mid-scene.

options: You own the copyright because you paid for the subscription
The platform's terms transfer full copyright to you automatically
No copyright vests without sufficient human authorship (US Copyright Office position), a commercial license is use rights, not copyright, and distributors want chain of title
Copyright doesn't matter for festival films
questions.q: You scored your commercial film with AI music from a paid Suno account. A distributor asks for proof of rights / chain of title. What's the trap?
questions.why: A commercial license is not copyright. No copyright without sufficient human authorship, the platform's license gives you a contractual right to use the output, but distributors, insurers, and festivals ask for chain of title, and an AI track produces a thin file.

options: Studio monitors only, that's the professional standard
Your phone only, that's what audiences use
Skip QC; the mix is fine if it sounds fine once
Three-device listen plus the silence test, the chapter's mix QC
questions.q: Your mix sounds great on studio monitors but muddy on a phone. What QC does the chapter require?
questions.why: Mix QC: the three-device listen (monitors, headphones, phone/small speaker) plus the silence test. If it only works on one device, the mix isn't done.

options: Louder is always better
Balance dialogue first, then effects, then music, and leave headroom; loudness is a delivery spec, not a creative choice
Normalize everything to the same level
Mix in mono only
questions.q: What's the chapter's mix-balance discipline?
questions.why: Dialogue-first balance: dialogue leads, effects support, music beds underneath, with headroom preserved. Loudness targets are delivery specs to hit at export, not creative choices to chase in the mix.

options: Set the "Altered content" / "AI use" toggle in YouTube Studio, skipping risks platform labeling, removal, or YPP suspension
Nothing, YouTube doesn't require disclosure
Only disclose if someone asks in the comments
Delete the video and re-upload until it passes
questions.q: You upload a photorealistic AI-generated short to YouTube. What must you do?
questions.why: YouTube requires the "Altered content"/"AI use" toggle for realistic AI-generated or meaningfully altered content. If skipped, the platform labels it itself, or removes it, or suspends YPP.

options: Yes, AI performances are eligible like any other
Only if the film discloses AI use in the credits
No, the 99th Academy Awards rules (May 2026) require acting nominations to be performances demonstrably performed by humans with consent
Only for the Best Picture category
questions.q: You want an acting nomination for your fully synthetic performer at the 99th Academy Awards. What do the rules say?
questions.why: The 99th Academy Awards rules (approved May 2026): AI tools 'neither help nor harm' a nomination, but acting nominations require performances demonstrably performed by humans with consent.

options: The NO FAKES Act, it's federal law
Nothing yet, the NO FAKES Act is proposed, not law. Do not present it as law
The TAKE IT DOWN Act, it covers all digital replicas
State likeness statutes always apply nationwide
questions.q: Someone claims a federal law already gives them rights against non-consensual digital replicas of themselves. True?
questions.why: The NO FAKES Act is proposed, not law. Do not present it as law. (The TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed 2025, is narrower: notice-and-removal for non-consensual intimate imagery.)

options: No disclosure needed, it's just an ad
A handshake agreement with the actor's estate
Only platform disclosure on X
Conspicuous disclosure under NY General Business Law § 396-b(3), $1,000 first violation, $5,000 each subsequent (confirm with counsel)
questions.q: Your New York ad campaign uses a synthetic performer. What's legally required?
questions.why: NY General Business Law § 396-b(3): ads containing a synthetic performer (with actual knowledge) must conspicuously disclose it. Penalties: $1,000 first, $5,000 subsequent. Penalty figures are single-source, confirm with counsel.

options: Publish freely, EU law doesn't apply to video
Disclose AI generation: the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duty applies to AI-generated media that could pass for real, regardless of platform policy
Only disclose if the platform asks
Geo-block the EU and ignore it
questions.q: You publish AI-generated video that could pass for real to a European audience. What does the chapter say about the EU AI Act?
questions.why: EU AI Act Article 50: legal transparency duty for anyone publishing AI-generated images, audio, or video that could pass for real, applies regardless of platform policy. Deployer obligations took effect August 2026. (Single-source summary, verify against the official EU text.)
